result: The authors developed and validated a 61-question bilingual survey on cervical cancer screening and management during COVID-19, piloted with 21 Canadian experts through three iterative rounds, and distributed via professional societies and online platforms between November 2020 and February 2021.
evaluation: Claims C17-C27 provide comprehensive methodological details about survey development, validation, translation, distribution channels, and timeline. The pilot testing with experts (C18-C19) and multi-platform distribution strategy (C20-C26) demonstrate rigorous survey methodology. The $5 incentive (C27) is a standard practice for survey research.

result: Of 778 respondents who clicked the survey link, 510 were included in the final analysis after excluding 235 ineligible surveys and 33 questionable responses, with a median completion time of 11 minutes 53 seconds.
evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are directly supported by Figure 1 and text describing the survey flow and quality control measures. The exclusion criteria (C29-C30) are clearly defined and appropriate for ensuring data quality. The completion time (C32) provides evidence of survey feasibility.

result: Survey respondents were predominantly female (55.7%), with a mean age of 44.4 years, primarily from Ontario (41.0%), British Columbia (21.0%), and Alberta (12.8%), with most being general practitioners/family physicians (43.7%) working in private clinics (32.9%).
evaluation: Claims C34-C39 are directly supported by Table 1 and provide essential demographic characterization of the survey sample. The overlap between colposcopists and gynecologists (C39) is appropriately noted and important for interpreting results.

result: Widespread disruptions in cervical cancer screening appointments occurred during early COVID-19, with 63.7% reporting cancellations and 74.9% reporting postponements, primarily affecting family physicians in private clinics in Ontario, with most appointments deferred by less than 4 months.
evaluation: Claims C40-C52 and C118, C120 are consistently supported by Table 2 and Figures 2-6, showing substantial disruptions across the screening continuum. The data on who initiated cancellations (physician/institution vs. patient) and conversion to telemedicine provide important context. The finding that appointment scheduling was most severely impacted (C118) is well-supported by the high cancellation/postponement rates.

result: Cervical cancer screening test volumes decreased substantially during the pandemic, with 76.1% of respondents using cytology and 15.8% reporting ≥75% decrease in Pap tests, while delays in scheduling were reported by 56.9% for Pap tests, 22.6% for HPV tests, and 21.8% for co-tests.
evaluation: Claims C53-C61 are supported by the text and Supplementary file 2b-2d, documenting substantial decreases in screening test volumes. The differential impact on different test types (Pap vs. HPV vs. co-tests) is consistently reported. However, the manuscript lacks statistical testing to determine if differences between test types are significant.

result: One-third of respondents (33%) indicated the pandemic would facilitate HPV self-sampling implementation, with 50.1% favoring it as an alternative screening method, though 30 respondents (primarily primary care providers in Ontario private clinics) were unfamiliar with the approach.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C93-C95, C116-C117 are supported by text, Table 6, and Figures 14-15. The finding that HPV self-sampling could address pandemic challenges (C116-C117) is logical but represents inference rather than demonstrated evidence. The substantial proportion unfamiliar with HPV self-sampling (C94-C95) highlights an important knowledge gap, particularly among primary care providers.

result: Colposcopy and follow-up appointments were also disrupted, with 25.2% reporting colposcopy cancellations, 37% reporting postponements, 33.3% reporting follow-up cancellations, and 53.5% reporting follow-up postponements, along with delays in receiving test results from laboratories.
evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are supported by Supplementary files 2f-2h and Figures 8-9 with supplements. The lower rates of colposcopy disruptions compared to screening appointments may reflect prioritization of diagnostic procedures, though this interpretation is not explicitly tested. The delays in laboratory result reporting (C68-C70) represent an additional source of care disruption.

result: Telemedicine was widely adopted, with 89.5% of respondents reporting their practice/institution used it to communicate with patients, and 72.7% reporting virtual consultations were covered by public health insurance, with test results reporting (82.1%) and health history reporting (66%) deemed most appropriate for telemedicine conversion.
evaluation: Claims C71-C79 and C119 are directly supported by Table 3 and demonstrate rapid telemedicine adoption during the pandemic. The high rate of insurance coverage (C74) likely facilitated adoption. The appropriateness ratings for different interactions (C75-C79) provide practical guidance, though these represent opinions rather than evidence of telemedicine effectiveness.

result: Respondents reported both over-screening/over-diagnosis/over-treatment (44.5% of responses, with over-diagnosis at 20.1% being most common) and under-screening/under-diagnosis/under-treatment (81.9% of responses) existed pre-COVID-19, with pandemic delays potentially having negative impacts by reducing necessary screening (47.8%), diagnosis (48.4%), and treatment (25.3%).
evaluation: Claims C80-C85 are supported by Table 4 and reveal important nuances in provider perspectives. The coexistence of concerns about both over- and under-screening (C80, C82) suggests heterogeneity in pre-pandemic practice patterns. However, these are subjective assessments without objective data on actual rates of over/under-screening, and the manuscript does not address the apparent contradiction of simultaneous over- and under-screening concerns.

result: By the time of survey completion, 45.1% of respondents reported catching up with pandemic-related cancellations/postponements, though 51.3% reported patients were not returning at pre-COVID capacity, with 32.3% noting increased frequency of patients with worsened symptoms and 16.6% reporting 25-49% of patients diagnosed with more advanced abnormalities.
evaluation: Claims C86-C92 are supported by Table 5 and Figure 13, documenting incomplete recovery and concerning trends in disease severity. The finding that nearly half had caught up (C86) while half reported patients not returning (C89) suggests differential recovery across settings. The increased severity findings (C91-C92) are particularly concerning but represent provider perceptions rather than systematic data on stage at diagnosis.

result: Recovery efforts were limited, with 36.2% reporting no measures implemented to catch up with delays, 24.7% experiencing 2-4 month service interruptions, and 13.1% experiencing >6 month interruptions, while most practices followed governmental (63.5%) or professional association (17.3%) screening guidelines.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 are supported by Table 6 and highlight substantial variation in pandemic response and recovery. The lack of catch-up measures in over one-third of practices (C96) is concerning. The prolonged service interruptions (C97-C98) likely contributed to the disease severity concerns noted in other claims. Guideline adherence data (C99-C100) provides context for practice patterns.

result: The manuscript contextualizes findings within extensive prior literature documenting pandemic impacts on cancer care globally, including screening declines of 35-87%, decreased cancer diagnoses, treatment delays, and modeling predictions of increased cancer cases and deaths.
evaluation: Claims C1-C16 and C101-C115 are all supported by appropriate citations to peer-reviewed literature and provide essential context for interpreting the survey findings. The consistency of findings across multiple countries and cancer types strengthens the validity of the reported disruptions. However, these are all citation-based claims about prior work rather than original findings from this study.
